In brief Would several superintelligent machines protect humans, exploit them, or eliminate them? In my models each outcome can happen, and the number of machines alone never decides which. In the two-machine model, rivals can guard more than humans could hold on their own only when three conditions hold together. The model assumes humans cannot win a war, either machine can grab only the whole human share, the machines cannot grab it together, and there is no prize for being strictly first. When war between the machines is cheap, rivalry can leave humans less than a single united bloc of machines would. If a full war between the machines would be too costly for either to fight, that guarding ends. The rivals can still pay humans to align with them as clients. Without defense by limited war, the model caps those payments at what humans can defend themselves. These are bounds on what is safe, not predictions, and no quantity in them has been measured for any real machine.

Part 1. More machines can protect humans or endanger them

In Measures That Depend on Ends I recommend keeping many centers of control before any single machine dominates. By that I mean human institutions: authority over critical infrastructure spread across many hands, and independent oversight. That recommendation does not answer a different question, the one I take up here: what several machines do to one another and to us. More independent machines are also more players with strategies of their own. They can collude at the expense of weaker actors. They can deadlock over rank. They can fight wars that sweep up bystanders or treat them as battlegrounds.

So when does a world of more than one machine help humanity, and when does it hurt? Five questions organize the analysis:

  1. If several machines are in the field, do they merge into a single bloc or stay rivals, and what does each arrangement leave humanity?
  2. When would one machine go to war with another to stop it from seizing what humans hold?
  3. How does status shape things, both as a running concern with a rival’s share and as a prize for being strictly first?
  4. If rival machines keep each other from fighting a full war, as the Cold War superpowers did under mutual deterrence, do humans become clients worth courting, and what does courting pay?
  5. When do rival machines actually protect humanity?

Throughout, “what a machine wants” stands for what the technical paper calls its ends. Across the models, protection, exploitation and elimination are all possible. The count of machines by itself never settles which one happens.

Part 2. How the models are built, and what they take as given

Five starting points from earlier work

Rather than re-derive results from other papers of mine in this series, I take five starting points as given.

  • The War Baseline, on one machine facing one humanity, studies two ways bargaining breaks down: hidden information, and power that shifts from round to round. Both are set aside here. In the basic game everyone knows everything relevant, and all choices happen in a single round.
  • Ends, Rank and Conflict, on status and what machines want, scores a machine by its own share minus a fixed weight times the other side’s share. There, how much an agent cares about relative standing (the technical term is positionality) is treated as an empirical feature of what it wants, to be measured. Here I split that weight in two: one toward a rival machine and one toward humanity.
  • Takeoff and Emergence, on how a second machine can arise, shows that follower machines exist and can still combine against a leader only when the leader has no decisive lead and no preventive strike pays while the followers are emerging. Here I start with two or more machines already in the field and do not model how the second one arrives.
  • Satiation Is Not Enough proves two results about one machine facing an outside risk of being destroyed. The model considers one opportunity to strike per period, with the risk in that period, its hazard, set separately at each of a series of distinct holding levels. If that risk never falls as its holdings grow, a machine whose wants can be satisfied can credibly promise to stop expanding, whatever fighting costs (Theorem A). If larger holdings buy safety and fighting is cheap, no promise to stop short of domination is credible, however satisfiable its wants (its Theorem C). I also treat humanity’s own trouble making promises across many communities there.
  • Humanity is treated as a single player, except in Part 9 and a few extensions. Changing the Ends, another paper in the series, questions that assumption.

The basic game: three players dividing one prize

Picture two machines, call them A and B, and humanity, dividing a single prize that can be cut any way. Each holds a share, and the shares add up to the whole.

Each machine values its own share, and it may also mind what others hold. I call how much a machine minds its rival machine’s share its rival weight, and how much it minds humanity’s share its human weight. Each runs from zero (it does not care) to one (it minds another’s gain as much as it values its own). Humanity may likewise mind what the machines hold. Shares measure resources, not welfare, and the models leave out war casualties.

Fixed weights are a choice I make with open eyes. Powell (1991) argues against assuming that states value relative gains for their own sake. He shows that such concern can arise from the cost and technology of force, even among actors who care only about their own payoffs. I keep fixed weights because Ends, Rank and Conflict treats them as a feature of what an agent wants, to be measured rather than derived. Snidal (1991) likewise fixes a relative-gains weight “as an assumption”. In his version, the weights across rivals add up to at most one and are diluted equally among them. Where results extend beyond two machines, every rival gets the full rival weight rather than a diluted one.

The rules of play adapt a model by Gallop (2016) to a prize that can be cut any way. An existing division is on the table, and humanity keeps its share unless attacked. Each player either accepts or attacks one other player. The third player, the bystander, then decides whether to join the war, and joins only if that leaves it strictly better off. A deal holds when, given how the bystander would respond, no player prefers any attack to the deal. Everyone knows everything relevant, and promises within the single round are assumed to be kept.

Two kinds of war

War in the basic game comes in two forms.

  • General war. Any war involving both machines is a general war (the technical paper’s decisive war). Its single winner is drawn by lot, with odds in proportion to the fighters’ strength. The winner takes the entire prize, humanity’s share included. Part 10 calls this kind of proportional lottery a ratio contest, as opposed to a decisive contest, in which the stronger side simply wins.
  • Seizure. A machine that attacks humanity alone takes all of humanity’s share. Taking all or nothing is an assumption; if a machine could take part of the share, the protected window described in Part 4 could narrow. The seizure goes through unless the rival machine steps in to defend, which turns it into a general war.

Fighting has costs. Each machine pays a cost of general war. A machine that seizes humanity’s share alone pays a seizure cost: what humans can make a grab cost. Humanity pays its own cost if it fights. In the baseline, each cost counts only against whoever pays it. Under an alternative, the rival-losses rule, a machine also counts its rival’s war cost as a gain to itself; I note where that changes a result.

Humanity’s weight has two separate parts. One is fighting strength, which is set to zero in most of the two-rival models. The other is the seizure cost. Even with no chance of winning a war, humans can make a grab costly.

When a human share counts as safe

A human share is safe when two things hold. First, machine peace: neither machine prefers a general war to the deal. Second, for each machine, either its rival would defend humanity against a seizure, or seizing is not worth the seizure cost.

Three modelling choices shape the results. A bystander keeps its own share during a war against humanity alone. (Part 5 checks, for whether deals exist at all, an alternative in which the winner of any two-player war also takes the bystander’s share.) Seizure is all or nothing. And the two machines cannot loot humanity together and split the take. A fourth choice works against rivals: the winner of a general war takes humanity’s share without paying the seizure cost, whereas a bloc that seizes must pay it.

How the results are checked

Many of the formal results are checked by a proof-checking program (Lean 4). Such a program confirms that a conclusion follows from the stated assumptions, not that the assumptions hold in the world. Here it checks the algebra of the conditions as written: payoffs, who accepts, who joins, and who seizes. Many of the checked statements are one-step rearrangements of a definition. That those conditions follow from the full game is checked by hand when humanity has no fighting strength, and the program does confirm that humanity then never gains by attacking. When humanity has some strength, the link is checked numerically against the full three-player game, not by formal proof. Tables, random samples and worked examples are computed by script. Readings of evidence, and premises not yet tested, are flagged as conjectures.

Each later model changes one thing

After the basic game, each part changes or replaces one piece. No single workable model captures every setting in which several machines and humanity might meet, so rather than force incompatible assumptions into one framework, I keep these games apart. Part 5 adds a prize for being strictly first. Part 6 gives humanity fighting strength and lets it pledge to defend whichever machine is attacked. Part 7 puts the machines in mutual deterrence and adds payoffs for courting humans as clients and for limited wars over them. Part 8 turns to a single dominant machine deciding whether to keep humanity. Part 9 splits humanity into many communities. Part 10 uses three separate models with a single calculation at a time. It asks when a machine tries to dominate all the others, when a third party can switch sides to keep one of two blocs from dominating, and how strength fades over distance. A grid in the technical paper’s appendix maps all these cases by number of machines and number of human communities, and shows how much of the general problem remains open.

Part 3. In my model, a united bloc leaves powerless humans at most what they can make a grab cost, and less if it minds human holdings

Suppose the two machines’ wants converge, so that they act toward humanity as a single bloc, each counting the other’s share as its own. The three-player game then becomes a two-player bargain between the bloc and humanity. For any chance the bloc has of winning a war, two conditions govern a deal. The bloc accepts leaving humanity a share if and only if that share, multiplied by one plus the bloc’s human weight, is no more than humanity’s chance of winning (multiplied by that same factor) plus the cost the bloc pays in that war, the seizure cost. Humanity accepts if and only if its share, multiplied by one plus how much it minds machine holdings, is at least its chance of winning (multiplied by that factor) minus its cost of fighting.

Under the baseline cost rule, a peaceful deal that leaves humanity something always exists in this bargain, provided humanity can make a seizure cost the bloc something and fighting costs humanity something too. The limit comes when humanity has no chance of winning a war. Then the bloc leaves a share alone only if that share, multiplied by one plus the bloc’s human weight, is no more than the seizure cost.

So the largest safe share is the seizure cost, scaled down the more the bloc minds human holdings, and never more than the whole prize. I call this the bloc bound. As an analogy only: a shop whose sole protection is the trouble a robbery would cause can safely keep on the counter only what that trouble outweighs, and less if the robber resents the shopkeeper.

The result is a ceiling, not a forecast. Nothing in it says which share inside the bound humanity actually receives. And a deal can fail outright. Under the rival-losses rule, if the bloc counts humanity’s war cost as a large enough gain to itself, it rejects every share and no deal exists. The gain must exceed the seizure cost plus humanity’s chance of winning multiplied by one plus the bloc’s human weight. Under that rule, a deal can also fail when the least humanity would accept is more than the most the bloc would leave.

Part 4. In my baseline model, two rivals can guard more than a bloc, but only when three conditions hold together

Now suppose the machines stay rivals. Can one machine’s readiness to check the other protect a human share larger than the bloc bound? In the two-machine model it can, under three conditions that must all hold together. Under other conditions rivalry leaves humanity worse off than a bloc would. All of this assumes all-or-nothing seizure, no joint seizure, no prize for being strictly first, and a humanity with no fighting strength.

Peace between the machines

Start with machine peace alone, setting seizure aside. A split of the non-human part that both machines find at least as good as general war exists exactly when four conditions hold together:

  1. Humanity’s share is no more than the whole.
  2. Humanity’s share, multiplied by one minus the rival weight plus twice the human weight, is no more than their two war costs combined.
  3. If A got everything humanity does not hold, A would find that deal at least as good as war.
  4. If B got everything humanity does not hold, B would find that deal at least as good as war.

Two directions follow. Lowering the human weight, so the machines mind human holdings less, never shrinks the range of human shares that allow machine peace. Under the baseline cost rule, raising the rival weight never shrinks it either. The second condition, notably, does not depend on which machine is stronger. Under the rival-losses rule things shift: raising the rival weight can tighten that condition when the machines mind human holdings at all, while when they do not and the rival weight is below one, the rival weight drops out of that condition altogether. In the four peace conditions, each machine subtracts the gain it counts from its rival’s war cost from its own war cost. If the machines mind human holdings and their combined war cost is positive, raising the rival weight strictly tightens the second condition.

Guardianship

Machine peace is not enough, because each machine must also refrain from grabbing humanity’s share. Suppose A grabs and B stands aside. B then faces a rival that has absorbed humanity’s share. B steps in when a general war looks better to it than that. When this readiness to defend is what keeps a share above the bloc bound safe, I call it guardianship.

Guardianship needs three conditions at once:

  1. Each machine minds its rival’s gains more than humanity’s holdings. The reason is simple. B accepts the deal, so for B the deal is at least as good as war. B would also rather fight than let A absorb humanity’s share. Both can be true only if A getting the share hurts B more than humanity holding it does. When the rival weight is no larger than the human weight, rivals never guard a share that a bloc would not leave alone.
  2. Neither machine is hopeless. A machine is hopeless when its odds in a general war, multiplied by one plus its rival weight, are no more than its war cost. Then nothing short of war leaves it worse off than war would, so it never defends, and every safe deal is capped at the bloc bound. With equal war costs, guardianship needs the weaker machine’s odds, multiplied this way, to beat the war cost. It does not need near-equal strength.
  3. Humanity’s share sits in a window. It must be large enough that each machine would fight a general war to defend it. With equal war costs, that means the share, multiplied by one plus the rival weight, exceeds twice the war cost. It must also be small enough not to tempt a general war over the division itself, so machine peace and the best-case conditions above must hold. For two equal machines, the model gives the exact answer. A share is safe when machine peace holds and the share is either within the bloc bound (humans defend it themselves) or above the window’s lower edge (the rival guards it).

When war between them is cheap enough, even a lopsided pair can guard humanity. Take a pair where A wins a general war 90 times in 100, the war cost is 0.1, the seizure cost is 0.05, the rival weight is 0.5 and the human weight is zero. A human share of 0.25 is safe in both the two-machine conditions and the computed three-player game. That is five times the bloc cap of 0.05. In the two-machine conditions the guarded shares run from just above 0.133 up to 0.25, where A’s best-case condition holds exactly and B gets nothing.

Two surprises

The first surprise is an unsafe middle. Whenever the bloc bound sits below the window’s lower edge, there is a band of shares between the two where no deal is safe between equal rivals. This band includes the window’s lower edge itself and starts just above the bloc bound. A share there is too large for the seizure cost to deter a grab. Yet it is too small to make the rival pay for a general war to stop the grab. (Or, when the rival weight is below the human weight, the share can be too large for machine peace.) So a larger share inside the window can be safe where a smaller one in the middle is not. As an analogy only: a night watchman who turns out for a large theft but not a small one makes a small purse less safe than a big one. Figure 1 lays out the self-defended shares, unsafe middle and guarded window for case 1 of the table below.

The second surprise is that rivalry can be worse than a bloc. When war between the machines is cheap enough relative to a positive seizure cost, the ceiling on human shares that machine peace allows sits strictly below the bloc bound, making the bloc bound itself unsafe between rivals (given a seizure cost of at most one plus the human weight). For equal rivals, the exact test is whether twice the war cost, multiplied by one plus the human weight, is less than the seizure cost multiplied by one minus the rival weight plus twice the human weight. The reason is the fourth modelling choice: the winner of a general war takes humanity’s share without paying the seizure cost. And if the machines mind human holdings at least as much as they mind each other’s, rivals never protect more than a bloc.

The table shows these cases. It is computed, and it compares the bloc bound with the safe shares for two equal rivals, worked out two ways.
