Guardianship rests on ruling out a joint grab

Allowing the machines to loot humanity together can shrink or erase the guardianship window. The rules allow only one-on-one attacks, with no joint seizure and no side payments. Suppose instead the two could seize humanity’s share jointly, at a total cost equal to the seizure cost, and divide the take and the cost as they chose. Then safe shares would be capped at the seizure cost divided by one minus the rival weight plus twice the human weight (the same multiplier as in the second machine-peace condition). Below the cap, no division of the take and cost makes both machines better off than the deal. Above it, dividing both equally would make both machines better off. Any part of the window would survive only when that cap sits above the window’s lower edge. (Both points are derived by hand.)

Under that cap the 90-to-10 example fails, because the cap of 0.10 is below 0.25 and below the window’s lower edge of 0.133. In case 1 the cap is 0.100, which leaves nothing of the window. In case 5 the cap is 0.167, which leaves shares from just above 0.105 to 0.167, about a tenth of the window’s width. Those survive only for divisions that leave the bystander at least its deal payoff. In case 6 the cap is 0.056, again leaving nothing.

How this relates to earlier work

In substance, guardianship is a known idea placed in a new setting. Gallop (2016) found a kind of deal kept in place by a threat to fight, in which “the threat of violence may be the only way to preserve peace”. Here one machine’s readiness to join a war against a seizer is what preserves humanity’s share. What I add here is the window of safe shares, its unsafe middle, and the comparison with a bloc. Signorino and Tarar (2006) estimated 58 extended-deterrence crises between states (where one state tries to deter an attack on another). Their estimates are consistent with the defender’s threshold here, including the hopeless-defender effect. But they model an allied defender, not a rival that suffers a loss of standing.

Part 5. In my model, a prize for being strictly first can make equal machines fight

Status can enter in a second way: as a fixed rank prize for whichever machine holds strictly more, whether in the deal or by winning a war. A tie pays each machine a tie value of at most half the prize. Among states, Wohlforth (2009) attributes to superpowers in a two-power system a preference for “an ambiguous status quo in which neither is dominant” over being “unambiguously outranked”. In the model, that preference is a positive tie value. As in Part 4, humanity has no fighting strength in this rank model.

One part of this is not solved: seizure under a rank prize. Grabbing humanity’s share can change who is strictly first. So a rank prize can make a bystander defend outside Part 4’s conditions. It can also tempt a machine to grab a small share, below the bloc bound, just to take first place (derived by hand).

For machine peace between near-equal machines, the two forms of status pull in opposite directions. Under the baseline cost rule, the rival weight widens the room for peace. A rank prize worth more than twice the tie value narrows it. For two equal machines, the amount by which the prize exceeds twice the tie value comes straight off the room for peace. More precisely, a split allows machine peace exactly when the human share, multiplied by one minus the rival weight plus twice the human weight, is no more than twice the war cost plus twice the tie value minus the rank prize.

When the prize exceeds twice the war cost plus twice the tie value, equal machines have no peaceful deal at any human share, even when humanity holds nothing. This assumes deals are fixed divisions; a lottery over first place could restore a bargain (derived by hand). The reason is that no division can make up to the second-place machine for losing the prize without putting it first instead. Splitting the prize in an even tie pays each machine only the tie value from rank, which is less than the rank payoff it expects from gambling on war: half the rank prize, less the war cost.

This gives a counterpart to the conflict among equals that Wohlforth (2009) argues for in words, using historical evidence he calls exploratory. His argument draws on how group identity shapes reactions to status and how different kinds of power can imply different ranks. There are two differences. In his account, a flat hierarchy breeds conflict through uncertainty about rank and mismatched kinds of power. Here, with complete information, equal war costs and a fixed division, machines equal in a single kind of power deadlock when the prize for strict first place exceeds twice the war cost plus twice the tie value.

When the hierarchy is steep, peace returns at humanity’s expense. If the weaker machine’s war odds are poor enough, given its war cost, its rival weight and the rank prize, it accepts a deal giving the stronger machine everything and humanity nothing. That same condition makes the weaker machine hopeless, so guardianship is gone too. The condition is sufficient, not exact.

How exact is the steep-hierarchy condition? When humanity holds nothing and war costs are equal, the model gives an exact threshold (written out in the technical paper) for deals that put one machine strictly first. That threshold is also exact for all deals when ties pay nothing and the machines are strictly unequal. With a positive tie value, an even tie can be accepted even where the threshold fails. One example: the stronger machine’s odds are 0.55, the prize is 1, the tie value is 0.5, the war cost is 0.1, and neither weight applies. For unequal machines in general, the exact conditions agree with a check of a grid of possible splits in 5,999 of 6,000 randomly drawn cases. The grid missed one interval about 2.4 millionths wide. This is computed.

Does a third player by itself cause deadlock?

In Gallop’s (2016) model of bargaining over policy, with three players “war is an equilibrium”. When three actors want different policies, “any bargain that would satisfy two of the three players is worse than war for the third player” (Gallop 2016). For bargaining over “a unit of goods”, a footnote in the 2016 working-paper copy used here (which lacked its proof appendix) says that “there will always be a way of dividing the good such that all players will prefer to go to war” (Gallop 2016). I read “go to war” there as standing for preferring the division to war, because the next sentence contrasts the point with Ray’s (2009) finding that excludable goods (goods others can be shut out of) are more prone to conflict than public goods. That reading is an inference from the working-paper copy alone, and I make no claim about the published article.

Numerical checks of the three-player game point to the same distinction. They use the main war rules, the baseline cost rule and no rank prize. When humanity has no fighting strength, the split that gives each machine its war odds and humanity nothing is safe (derived by hand). When humanity has some strength, every case had a peaceful deal across 1,500 draws that sampled the parameter ranges uniformly and 3,000 draws designed to test extreme settings. This is computed evidence within the samples drawn, not a universal proof.

The deadlocks that did turn up in the samples came from three specific sources:

  • Strict rank between near-equals: the deadlock over first place described above.
  • The rival-losses rule: about half of random draws with status concerns had no deal. But 9,529 of the 9,645 failures already failed with humanity powerless, a two-player effect. Only 116 instances (1.2 percent) needed humanity’s weight to tip the game into deadlock.
  • A status-driven spoiler under the alternative war rules, where the winner of any two-player war also takes the bystander’s share. No failures appeared in 20,000 random draws or in 30,000 draws without status concerns. But 128 of 40,000 stress draws produced a genuine three-player deadlock. In those, a weak player that strongly minds a dominant one’s gains attacks to set off a general war that the third player might win.

So over a prize of resources that can be cut any way, and under the baseline cost rule, adding a third player did not by itself break peace in these samples. Gallop’s three-player deadlock remains possible when players dispute a shared rule or policy that cannot be split or settled by dividing resources, as discussed in The War Baseline.

Part 6. In my model, a human pledge to defend whichever machine is attacked adds little when humans are weak

Now give humanity some fighting strength. Let no one care about relative standing. And suppose humanity tries to play kingmaker by pledging to join whichever machine the other attacks.

To isolate the logic of such a pledge, this model swaps in a different war rule. If humanity joins a defending machine, the defending side wins with odds in proportion to the defender’s and humanity’s combined strength. The prize goes to the defending machine. That machine honors humanity’s deal share afterward only with some chance, its commitment. A machine that wins without humanity’s help owes humanity nothing. (Under the earlier rule, humanity could win the whole prize for itself, so joining a war could make sense even with no machine commitment, whenever humanity’s share of total strength exceeds its cost of fighting.)

Three results follow:

  1. The military swing is bounded by humanity’s share of total strength. Joining the defender raises the defender’s odds, but never by more than humanity’s share of all the strength in the field.
  2. With a pledge that humans would honor for either defender, the bound set by the machines’ combined war costs rises by exactly humanity’s share of total strength. Each machine’s separate bound rises by less and can still limit the human share. This concerns machine peace only. Seizure of humanity is not modelled here, and adding a seizure limit could leave no share that is both peaceful and covered by a credible pledge.
  3. Without machine commitment, the pledge is not credible. For humanity to be willing to defend either machine, the machines must keep their word with some positive chance. Humanity’s share, discounted by that chance and by the weaker defending side’s odds of winning, must also outweigh humanity’s cost of fighting. That requirement can leave no workable share even when the machines are certain to keep their word. With no commitment at all, no share makes the pledge credible.

When humanity is weak next to the machines, the kingmaker effect adds almost nothing to what humanity can hold. Snyder (1965) saw a parallel shift in the nuclear era: in the balance of terror between two superpowers, the threat to “raise the ante” replaced “the threat to recruit additional states” as the core of balancing. Under mutual deterrence in this model, the reason to court a militarily weak humanity is the value it can bring, for example by providing private information as an asset or conferring standing as an audience.

Part 7. In my model, when machines deter each other without limited-war defense, rivals may court humans as clients, paying at most what humans can defend

Suppose a general war between the machines is so destructive that neither would ever fight one: it is worse for each machine than the worst peaceful outcome. In the model, neither machine has a reason to fight if its war cost is at least the size of the whole prize plus the larger of the rival and human weights plus the loss it counts when a rival gains a human client. During the Cold War, mutual assured destruction rested on nuclear forces that could survive a first strike. Snyder’s (1965) test of stability was the “distance” each superpower stood from “a full first-strike capability”. For machines, I conjecture that mutual deterrence would rest on keeping backup copies or spreading the learned values that govern the machine across locations. With the machines deterring each other at the top, humans, who pose no military threat, are in the position of newly independent states courted as clients.

This model adds assumptions outside the basic game:

  • A general war ends any client relationship.
  • Humanity’s alignment is worth some amount to the machine it joins, its patron, as an asset or audience. I call this its client value. Each rival machine counts the patron’s gain as a loss through its rival weight.
  • A patron can pay humanity a transfer out of its own share, raising humanity’s holdings.
  • Alternatively, a machine can start a limited proxy war over humanity. This means a limited war between machines, fought on human ground, over who holds humanity as a client, not a war handed off to local human forces. It costs each machine an assumed amount and destroys an assumed fraction of humanity’s holdings.

Five results

1. Mutual deterrence ends guardianship, because defending means fighting a general war. When general war is that costly, machine peace holds at every human share. But neither machine will ever fight to stop its rival from seizing humanity’s holdings. With a positive client value, the condition that guarantees machine peace is derived by hand, not machine-checked.

2. Patronage pays humans only what they can defend on their own. If seizure were impossible, competition among two or more machines would bid humanity’s price up to its full client value. At that price, winning and losing the client come out the same, and below it any rival gains by outbidding.

Under deterrence, though, a rival of the patron can seize the client. It takes the client’s holdings, including what the patron paid. It also wipes out the patron’s gain from the alliance, which the seizer counts as a gain through its rival weight. As a modelling choice, direct seizure destroys the client relationship, so the seizer gains no client value of its own; the winner of a proxy war, by contrast, keeps the client. (If seizure captured the client value too, the ceiling below would be lower still, derived by hand.) So a rival leaves the client alone if and only if the seizure cost covers both parts of what grabbing yields: the client’s holdings after the payment (multiplied by one plus the human weight) plus the rival’s loss from the alliance. When the seizure cost is low next to the client value, paying full value would invite the very seizure it pays for. This happens whenever the seizure cost is less than the full client value multiplied by one plus the human weight.

The model assumes complete information and a client that refuses any payment it cannot keep. Under those assumptions, what the client can defend and what its alignment is worth determine whether bidding is possible and how high it can go:

  • The price stops at the largest payment that still passes the seizure test, or at the full client value if that is smaller. This holds for any number of machines from two up, provided every machine holds enough to pay it.
  • When that stopping point is below full value, becoming a client lowers the most humanity can safely hold, below what it could safely hold unaligned. The drop is the rival’s loss from the alliance, divided by one plus the human weight. Yet accepting patronage raises humanity’s actual holdings by the payment and never lowers them compared with declining it.
  • If even a zero payment fails the seizure test, no client relationship survives at any price. Nothing is paid, and humanity stays unaligned, keeping its share provided that share is within the bloc bound.
  • If humanity is worth nothing as a client, no machine bids at all.

Yudkowsky and Soares (2025) argue that humans lack the leverage to be “worth including in trade or treaties”. I read only their pages 91–92 and six pages of their online supplement, not the rest of the work. The model agrees with them when humanity is worth nothing as a client. It also shows that even when humanity is worth something, patronage transfers no more than humanity’s own seizure cost can shield.

Why did Cold War superpowers not routinely seize each other’s clients? A human patron could defend its client by limited war, and this model leaves that option out. Whether deterred machines would defend clients that way is an open conjecture.

3. Competition can move onto human ground as a proxy war. Suppose ties among bidders are broken fairly, and either machine can start a proxy war before the tie is broken. The winner then holds the client at its reduced holdings, with no payment. Looking at one machine’s preference rather than a full equilibrium, a machine prefers starting the war to bidding when the war’s expected gain exceeds its cost. When a client deal passes the seizure test and every machine can afford the price, a machine that starts a war saves the payment in the cases where it would have won the bidding. It also values keeping the payment out of human hands and destroying some of what humans already hold. How much it values those two effects depends on its human weight. It shrinks the more the machine minds its rivals’ gains, since war also spares rivals from paying that price. (If a machine could instead start the war after losing the auction, the region where proxy war pays would be the same or wider. It would stay the same if the price were the full client value and widen if the seizure test kept the price below that value.) Even where no payment could pass the seizure test (though unaligned humanity is safe), a proxy war can still create a client worth keeping when it destroys enough of humanity’s holdings to make the remainder safe and its expected gain beats its cost.

For two machines, the effects of a more valuable client depend on whether humans can defend the full price:

  • Where they can, a stronger rival weight narrows the range where proxy war pays, a stronger human weight widens it, and a more valuable client raises the price and weakly widens that range (meaning it widens the range or leaves it unchanged). With two machines, a more valuable client definitely widens the range if the rival weight is below one or the machines put any weight on human holdings.
  • Where the full price is unsafe but a payment still passes the seizure test, a more valuable client lowers the safe price if the machines put any weight on a rival’s gain. It can narrow the range where starting a proxy war before the tie is broken would pay. It does narrow that range if the rival weight is positive and either the rival weight is below one or the machines also put weight on human holdings. (If the losing bidder can start the war after the auction, this direction reverses for two machines, derived by hand.) A stronger rival weight weakly narrows the range further, and the human weight cuts both ways.
  • Only with three or more machines can a very heavy rival weight reverse how client value shifts proxy war in both cases, and let a stronger rival weight widen the proxy-war range when humans cannot defend the full price. Here the rival weight is heavy enough when the weights on all the other machines add up to more than one plus the human weight counted once per machine. That depends on giving every rival the full, undiluted weight. Under Snidal’s (1991) diluted weights it cannot happen.

Snyder (1965) recorded the Cold War version of this shift: “the greater the stability of the ‘strategic’ balance of terror, the lower the stability of the overall balance at its lower levels of violence”. He endorsed it only “heavily qualified” by fear of escalation, and stated it for lower-level conflict between the same two powers; he traced peripheral internal wars instead to nuclear imbalance. Carrying this pattern over to machines and their human clients is my own step.

4. More machines shrink the proxy-war region. As the number of competing machines grows, each one’s chance of winning a proxy war falls, so proxy war pays in fewer cases. The price of patronage stays the same, as long as every machine holds enough to pay it. Because the machines’ shares together equal what humanity does not hold, any positive price also caps how many machines can meet that condition: at most the non-human share divided by that price. This does not cover machines that choose whether to enter, since bystanders could then stay out. Whether mutual deterrence itself stays stable among three or more machines is an open question. Snyder (1965) remarks that the balance of terror is “generally believed to be most stable when it is bipolar” and sets the many-power case aside.

5. Resource races can override courtship. Humans who pose no threat create no hazard for a machine, so the security motive against them vanishes. Holdings then buy no extra safety from humans, so a machine whose wants are satisfied can credibly stop expanding at any positive fighting cost under Theorem A. Between machines, though, larger holdings may lower the hazard a rival poses, and fighting may be cheap; that is the territory of Theorem C in Satiation Is Not Enough. A resource race then raises how much each extra unit of resources is worth. Results 2 to 4 hold that worth fixed. A race that raised it would also make payments costlier and lower the safe price.

Assume there is no way to take resources short of elimination. Then a race that raises the worth of resources can push the gain from elimination past the threshold. Once that gain crosses the threshold, valuing resources still more cannot reverse the elimination decision in the model. For the patron, it happens once the gain from eliminating the client exceeds the client’s value plus the cost of elimination; for a rival machine, keeping the client yields no client value, and denying that value to the patron adds to the gain from elimination. Where holdings can instead be cut to subsistence, the harm can be dispossession rather than elimination. Whether a machine race raises resource worth enough to matter is a conjecture. Still, Cold War superpowers did not need their clients’ territory to survive, and machines may need matter and energy.

In short, under mutual deterrence and without defense by limited war, the model gives humanity at most the reduced ceiling under patronage. Humanity can lose part of its holdings to proxy war. And if a resource race raises the worth of resources, it can face dispossession, or, assuming no way to take resources short of it, elimination.

Part 8. In my model, a lone dominant machine keeps humans when their value to it matches or exceeds its net gain from eliminating them

Now consider a single dominant machine that holds the field alone and decides whether to keep or eliminate humanity. Here the results are one-step consequences of how the machine’s accounting is defined.

Humans hold resources, measured in terms of what the machine wants. Eliminating humanity gains the machine three things:

  • Stake: humans hold matter, energy or computing power that the machine values.
  • Comparator: the machine ranks itself against human holdings, through its human weight.
  • Threat: eliminating humanity removes a danger to the machine (or, when a rival machine exists, denies that rival an asset).

Keeping humanity yields value in three possible roles. Humans can be an asset, generating or holding private information. They can be an audience, conferring standing or recognition. Or they can be an exhibit, a status good kept for display. Eliminating humanity also costs the machine something.

By definition, the machine eliminates humanity when the gains from stake, comparator and threat exceed humanity’s value in those roles plus the cost of elimination. This accounting is exact when resources are worth a constant amount per unit and approximate otherwise. The approximation values the whole change using what one more unit is worth at the machine’s current holdings. Here, as in Part 7, it assumes no way to take resources short of elimination.

Five implications follow here; a sixth, on many human communities, comes in Part 9:

  1. A pure knowledge end: if what the machine wants neither values what humans hold nor ranks itself against them, it eliminates humans if and only if their threat outweighs their value plus the cost of elimination. A caveat from Ends, Rank and Conflict applies. A race for priority in proving theorems is also a race for computing power, so any computing power humans hold gives the machine a stake in their resources. And a machine that measures its achievements against human mathematicians ranks itself against them.
  2. Without a threat, when humans’ value in those roles plus the cost of elimination is at least zero, elimination requires a stake or a comparator.
  3. A threat alone can suffice. Even with no stake and no comparator, a large enough threat leads to elimination. Conversely, humanity’s value as an asset, audience or exhibit protects it only if that value meets the full motive to eliminate less the cost of eliminating. Meeting that threshold is enough to protect humanity in this accounting.
  4. Being valuable to one machine can make humans a target for its rival. If a live rival values humanity, a machine that minds its rival’s gains counts destroying that value as a gain of its own. It eliminates humanity when that added gain and its other gains from elimination together exceed its own value for keeping humans plus the cost of eliminating them. The rival’s added reason to defend humanity is not modelled. Renshon (2016) finds a larger power advantage of initiator over target in military disputes for states dissatisfied with their status than for satisfied ones. That is a status-competition counterpart, not a test of this effect. It is also subject to the estimation caveat explained in Part 10, unless his statistical method builds strategic choices into the estimate, which I have not checked.
  5. A zoo keeps humans only at subsistence. Suppose the machine can cut human holdings to subsistence instead of eliminating humans, and the value of keeping them as an exhibit stays the same whatever their allotment. Then a dominant machine that values each unit of its own share equally does strictly worse at any allotment above the minimum needed to keep the exhibit alive. The zoo buys survival at subsistence, never a bargaining share. Whether the asset role, in which humans sustain private information in their own minds, requires genuine human autonomy is a conjecture that a single number cannot settle. Figure 2 pictures the keep-or-eliminate accounting as a balance.

Part 9. In my model, adding independent communities can weaken a unanimous shutdown threat and strengthen the rival-building threat

Now drop the assumption that humanity acts as one player. Consider one machine facing many separate human communities. Each community keeps the same capacity, so more communities mean more total independent capacity, not the same humanity cut more finely. (Dividing a fixed total capacity among more communities is a different case, not modelled; there the rival channel could weaken as numbers grow.)

The threat to the machine runs through two channels that respond to the number of communities in opposite ways:

  • The plug. Shutting the machine down requires every community to agree, and each is willing independently with some fixed chance. Unless every community is certain to be willing, the chance that all agree falls as communities multiply and tends to zero. If a few communities could pull the plug without the rest, the plug would grow stronger with numbers instead; the result depends on requiring unanimity.
  • The rival. Building a competing machine that defeats the incumbent needs only one community to succeed, so this chance rises as communities multiply.

The two combine into one hazard for the machine. The model multiplies the chance that no community builds a rival by the chance that the shutdown fails. Subtracting that joint chance from certainty gives the chance that at least one threat succeeds in the period. As an analogy only: a vote that needs everyone gets harder with more voters, while a lottery that needs one winner gets easier with more tickets. Figure 3 plots both chances, each community backing shutdown half the time and building a rival one time in ten.

How the hazard responds to the machine’s own growth matters, as Satiation Is Not Enough shows:

  • Tripwire. Suppose bigger holdings leave rival-building unchanged and do not make communities less willing to pull the plug. Then the hazard never falls as holdings grow. Combined with Theorem A, a machine with satisfiable wants can credibly promise to stop expanding, whatever fighting costs. Whether communities are hard to unite in calm times and easier to unite when a machine grabs is a conjecture.
  • Suppression. Suppose bigger holdings make rivals harder to build and leave willingness unchanged. Then the hazard at higher holdings is no higher. Where it strictly falls, the machine is in Theorem C’s territory, where no promise to stop short of domination is credible when fighting is cheap.
  • Both at once. If bigger holdings both suppress rivals and make communities more willing, while willingness stays short of certainty, suppression wins out once there are enough communities. The hazard at higher holdings is then the smaller one, though it still approaches certainty if any chance of building a rival remains, and approaches zero under complete suppression.

The plug weakens further when the call to act can be lost

My addition to this model is a reach cost. Willingness to pull the plug is not enough. Each community must also receive and read the call to coordinate, whereas a community building a rival needs no system-wide call. Suppose each community’s call passes through a chain of inboxes, its own included, and gets through each one with some fixed chance. If each chain is separate and every pass and every decision is independent, the chance that all communities are reached and willing is found by multiplying those chances. The model gives each chain the same number of inboxes at a given community count. For each community, multiply the pass chance once per inbox and then multiply by its chance of being willing. Multiply those results across all the communities.

Four properties follow from that multiplication:

  • The reach cost only weakens the plug. Lost messages never raise the machine’s hazard, since the rival channel is untouched.
  • The plug fades faster. If chains do not get shorter as communities multiply, the plug never strengthens with numbers. When communities have some chance of being willing and messages are not sure to get through, its ratio to the plug without losses shrinks toward zero as communities multiply.
  • The plug vanishes even if everyone is willing. With lossy inboxes, the plug tends to zero as communities multiply, even when every community is certain to be willing. Without losses, certain willingness would keep the plug certain at any size.
  • A weaker condition is enough. It suffices that each community’s call passes at least one lossy inbox on no other community’s chain, such as its own, and that those passes are independent and each get through with at most some fixed chance below certainty; multiplying that ceiling across communities then caps the plug and still sends it toward zero. If the passes are not independent, that cap is lost. In the extreme, when all the passes are one and the same event, the plug is higher than the multiplied form gives. The remaining ceiling is the pass chance for that one shared event.

Evidence here is thin. Sreedhar, Yuan, Chari, and Raskar (2026) simulated inbox forwarding in a 1,005-agent email network of language models. Their runs illustrate how passing messages along many hops under heavy traffic can drop delivery well below direct messaging. But the study is a preprint under review, with correlated cached outputs and experimental junk loads. The three links to this model are conjectures: that human coordination runs through such filters, on separate chains with independent passes, at a fixed rate.

Their runs also suggest attention capture. Under a fixed priority rule, spam backed by large deposits crowded out genuine requests. That is a plug-channel counterpart to the divide-and-conquer tactics Hui (2005) describes. If growing holdings let a machine buy down the rate at which calls get through, the effective plug can fall even as willingness rises, defeating the tripwire. If growth leaves rival-building unchanged and lowers neither willingness nor message delivery, the tripwire and its link to Theorem A stay intact.

A machine facing only a unanimous plug has a reason to avoid partial elimination

Return to Part 8’s dominant machine, now facing many communities. If threat, stake, value and cost all simply add up across communities and each unit of resources has a constant worth to the machine, the machine decides each community’s fate separately. Under a unanimous plug, though, the threat does not add up. Take the case where no community can build a rival and willingness is neither certain nor zero. Eliminating some communities raises the plug threat from those that remain, because fewer must agree. Eliminating all of them removes the plug altogether.

A machine facing only a unanimous plug therefore has a strategic reason to avoid partial elimination when it does not choose total elimination. When communities can also build rivals, the hazard can first fall and then rise as communities multiply: with a one-in-ten chance of building a rival and an even chance of willingness, the model’s hazard is 0.55, 0.39, 0.36 and 0.38 for one to four communities, and 0.65 at ten. Whether such a reason holds once communities can build rivals is a conjecture.

Part 10. Hegemony, balancing and distance: one-step models read against history

This part examines three separate one-step models, mostly simple rearrangements of their definitions, and reads them against the historical and quantitative record on international systems.

Two terms must stay strictly apart. A balance of power is a distribution of strength, such as parity between rivals. A balance-of-power system is an arrangement in which a dedicated balancer switches sides so that no one can dominate. Historians dispute whether even nineteenth-century Europe was a system of the second kind. Schroeder (1992) argues that the Vienna settlement of 1815–1848 rested on a shared British and Russian hegemony and a “political equilibrium” of agreed norms, not on a balancer. He calls Britain’s self-image as “the necessary disinterested holder of the balance” a way of “rationalizing its hegemonic role” (Schroeder 1992). Hui (2005) finds “no balancer in either early modern Europe or ancient China”, reading Britain’s role against Napoleon as “nothing more than the simple fact that Britain was France’s cohegemon”. Here, the balancer is a formal model, not a claim about European history.

In the baseline model, splitting the prize at the war odds beats bidding for hegemony whenever war costs anything

Scholars of states disagree about bids for dominance. On one side, Mearsheimer (2007) calls hegemony “the best way to guarantee survival”. Gilpin (1981) holds that dominant powers have not conceded dominance and rising powers have not held back. Organski and Kugler (1980) maintain that powerful challengers refuse subordinate status. On the other side, Waltz (1979) argues that a state’s “first concern … is not to maximize power”. Kirshner (2010) calls a bid for hegemony irrational for a state that wants to survive, given the risk of ruinous defeat. Wohlforth (1999) holds that the United States faces “only weak incentives to expand” because it “was the leading state in the Cold War, so the status quo already reflects its preferences”. For machines, Yudkowsky and Soares (2025) grant that rivals might settle into “a treaty and coordination rather than war”, but argue that a machine would still prefer not to split the galaxy with a rival if it could avoid it.

In the one-round basic game with full information and the baseline cost rule, splitting the prize at the war odds gives each machine strictly more than a war for hegemony, whenever war costs anything at all. (In that split, humanity gets nothing.) This matches Powell’s (1999) formal result that actors who want more and will run a “calculated risk” of war still settle at shares reflecting power whenever a peaceful bargain exists.

Within these models, a reason not to settle for half needs one of three departures:

  • A rank prize large enough that equal machines have no peaceful split (Part 5).
  • The rival-losses rule with cheap own war costs, where a machine’s own war cost is small next to how much it values the cost war inflicts on its rival. With humanity holding nothing, a peaceful split is impossible exactly when at least one machine’s counted gain from its rival’s war cost, less its own war cost, exceeds its rival’s chance of winning multiplied by one plus the rival weight.
  • Holdings that buy safety over time. When bigger holdings lower an outside hazard and fighting is cheap, Theorem C shows no promise to stop short of domination is credible. Takeoff and Emergence gives the condition under which a leader strikes an emerging follower first. The decision depends on the leader’s chance of winning the strike, how much it discounts future gains, its share once the follower arrives, and the cost of striking. Conversely, if a survivable second strike means holdings buy no safety against a rival hazard that never falls, Theorem A lets a machine with satisfiable wants credibly accept a split. Extending that from a fixed hazard to a strategic rival is a conjecture.

Balancing restrains a would-be hegemon only while the others can still beat or deter it

Suppose everyone else combines against a bidder holding some share of total strength, and no one cares about relative standing. Giving every player its strength share is then a peaceful deal. Every deal the bidder accepts leaves all the others combined, machines and humanity together, with at most their combined share of strength plus the bidder’s war cost. Peace holds with or without balancing; what balancing changes is the least the bidder will settle for. If bystanders stand aside instead (buck-passing, which Hui (2005) groups with other self-interested strategies that “facilitate domination”), the bidder’s odds against a single target rise, and so does that floor.

Yet even full balancing protects the rest very little once the bidder is overwhelming. The ceiling on what everyone else can keep approaches the bidder’s war cost as the bidder’s share of total strength approaches the whole. That is hegemony by bargain.

Nearly every account read here agrees, once its conditions are unpacked, that balancing restrains a would-be hegemon only while the others can still beat or deter it. Waltz (1979) notes that a balancer succeeds only if its weight is enough to tip the weaker side. Wohlforth (1999) defines a one-superpower world as the point where counterbalancing is impossible. Organski and Kugler (1980) argue that alliances cannot reverse power shifts driven by internal growth. Powell’s (1999) model, the only formal treatment among the sources read, concludes that “anarchy and the desire to survive do not produce a general tendency for states to balance”, with balancing deterring an attacker only in a narrow band of attacker odds (about 0.54 to 0.56). Against ancient Qin, Hui (2005) documents that “anti-Qin alliances formed very slowly and infrequently, they did not have enough members to overpower Qin, they rarely had unified command, and they readily disintegrated”. Once Qin had conquered more than half the system, Hui finds that even the combined strength of the other six states could not match it. For machines, whether followers exist and can still combine is the question Takeoff and Emergence answers.

A small human balancer can swing the outcome reliably when war is highly decisive and the blocs are nearly equal

Now let humanity act as balancer between two machine blocs. In a decisive contest, where the stronger side wins outright, humanity joining the weaker bloc flips the winner exactly when humanity’s weight exceeds the gap between the blocs. This matches Morgenthau’s (1948) requirement that the holder of the balance be “strong enough … to make likely the victory of whichever side it joined”. In a ratio contest, where each side wins with odds in proportion to strength, a weight above the gap likewise makes the weaker bloc the favorite. But it raises that bloc’s odds by no more than humanity’s share of the combined weight. For a fixed human weight and fixed combined strength of the machine blocs, the increase is larger when the stronger bloc holds more of that strength.

The table below is computed, and shows how much a balancer with weight 0.05 raises the weaker bloc’s chance of winning. The number on each row tells how much extra weight the contest gives a strength advantage. At 1, the odds are proportional to strength. At 64, even a small strength advantage can make a large difference to the odds. The columns vary the gap between the blocs.

How decisive war is Blocs equal Gap 0.02 Gap 0.1
1 (ratio contest) 0.024 0.024 0.026
4 0.094 0.097 0.096
16 0.321 0.369 0.140
64 0.498 0.903 0.002

A small humanity is pivotal near-certainly only when war between machine blocs is highly decisive and the blocs are close to equal. In a ratio contest it shifts the odds by at most its weight share.

A classical balancer, to avoid being absorbed as a prize, needed what Morgenthau (1948) called “threefold aloofness” and “virtual immunity from foreign attack”. Mearsheimer (2001) calls the equivalent advantage “the stopping power of water”. In the model, a balancer that cannot win a war on its own has one such moat: the seizure cost it can impose. The model covers humans with no fighting strength, or humans weaker than the stronger bloc in a one-on-one contest where the stronger side wins outright. Wherever no rival bloc would guard it, as under mutual deterrence or against a hopeless rival, humanity as balancer needs that cost of its own. Switching sides also requires humanity to solve the coordination problem of Part 9. It requires at least some chance that the defending bloc will honor its pledge, with Part 6 giving the further condition on when humans would join. And it fails if one machine’s rise is “great enough and … fast enough” (Kaplan, as excerpted in Hoffmann 1960).

Reverse the roles, with a machine balancing between two human blocs. Having enough weight to tip the outcome does not by itself mean the machine could beat both blocs together, or even one at a time. Whether a machine balancer stays a balancer rather than expanding is the question Satiation Is Not Enough addresses. (A machine facing a unanimous plug with no rival-building has reason to avoid eliminating one human bloc while leaving the other, as Part 9 showed; any such motive when rivals can be built is a conjecture.) History adds a warning about inviting a stronger outside power in. In the Hellenistic system, Greek balancing against Macedon “would have failed” without Rome, “which then proceeded to establish its own hegemony and swallow up the system” (Wohlforth et al. 2007). On my reading, that is an analogy for calling in one machine to balance another.

In the model, a large enough growth advantage can overcome distance losses if some strength still arrives

My starting hypothesis was that historical bids for hegemony failed for two main reasons. Either rivals balanced against the bidder, or the bidder’s strength ran thin as its supply lines stretched over distance. Balancing was modelled above. For distance, the model sets a hegemon projecting power over some distance against a local defender, under two ways that strength can fade:

  • A fixed loss per mile. The hegemon prevails only within a certain distance, set by its strength edge over the defender. If both sides grow by the same proportion, that distance brake erodes, and a hegemon that starts stronger eventually prevails at any fixed distance.
  • A fixed fraction arriving. If both sides grow by the same proportion, nothing changes. But if the hegemon grows enough faster than the defender (self-strengthening), it overcomes any such loss, as long as some of its strength arrives at all.

The historical record shows both brakes at work and how bidders got past them. Testing balance-of-power theory across eight pre-modern systems, Wohlforth et al. (2007) find effective balancing the exception, not the rule. Hegemony was likely “whenever a putative hegemon can make conquest pay and the system cannot expand to bring in new potential balancers”. Where bids stopped, the main causes were “limits on the putative hegemon’s ability to cumulate power”, together with the arrival of outside powers (Wohlforth et al. 2007). Their examples include Persian supply lines, Inca logistics, and the difficulty of Assyrian rule “over 1000 miles away”.

Hui (2005) names the same two brakes: “balance of power or resistance” (meaning balancing coalitions) and “rising costs of expansion or administration”. She shows how Qin overcame both “by pursuing counterbalancing strategies, ruthless stratagems, and self-strengthening reforms”. Over “Qin’s fifty-two expansionist wars from 356 to 221 bc”, Qin “met only eight allied responses”, because rivals preyed on one another and struggled to act together, while Qin split their coalitions. Balancing “merely slowed but did not check Qin’s rise to universal domination” (Hui 2005).

Qin’s reforms built direct rule and total mobilization over seven generations (135 years). Qin was largely “a borrower rather than an innovator”, and its reforms stood in contrast to the early modern European bidders crippled by “self-weakening expedients” such as mercenaries and tax farming (Hui 2005). Its edge “snowballed” as conquests paid and defeated rivals lost the means to rebuild. That edge matches outpacing growth in the model, though on my reading human mobilization of existing resources is a weaker analogue for compounding machine self-improvement.

On my reading, Qin got around distance in a way neither formula captures, even though Hui argues that Qin’s western location made projecting power over distance harder. By “befriending far-away [states] and attacking nearby [states]”, it advanced piece by piece and turned conquered land into “forward bases for targets further away” (Hui 2005). On my reading, that shortened the distance from its frontier rather than projecting power across a fixed span. For Hui, where expansion stops paying is “an empirical question that varies with contexts”, and a balance among self-strengthened states is “possible – though not likely”. She argues that balancing could be effective in Europe only because the drive for domination there was very weak. Defenders, in turn, can steepen the loss. Napoleon “had overcome the loss-of-strength gradient largely by using local supplies” until Spanish guerrillas denied them and forced France “to rely on supplies from home” (Hui 2005).

For machines on Earth, communication delay is negligible, and captured computing power, energy and code may build on themselves strongly. On my reading (not Wohlforth and colleagues’), strongly cumulative gains on a closed planet with no outside power to call in point toward hegemony under their conditions. Hui (2005) observes that after Napoleon, “developments in administrative and communication technologies significantly eased the mechanism of rising costs of expansion”. Only at cosmic scale does physics impose a loss no technology removes. Ord (2021) notes that the reachable universe has a shrinking radius, measured in present-day distances, of 16.5 billion light-years, beyond half of which round-trip signaling is impossible, raising problems of “coordinating these different outposts” and of values “drifting”. That hard cutoff provides no brake on Earth.

Why none of this ranks real systems

None of these results ranks real international systems by how stable they are. Two quantitative studies of system structure and war that I read here point in opposite directions.

For the period after 1945, which they code as “Bipolar/U.S. Hegemony”, Bennett and Stam (2004) estimate war risk at 4 percent and 1 percent of the pre-1918 risk. They call this “strong support for the neorealist claim”. They note, though, that the two-superpower era coincides with NATO, nuclear weapons and the United Nations, and that period markers “add little”. Between pairs of states, they find parity the most war-prone arrangement and a clear strength advantage for one side the least: “Creating locally equal balances of power increases these risks” (Bennett and Stam 2004).

Bueno de Mesquita and Lalman (1988) test structural measures across European major-power wars from 1816 to 1965. Structural variables alone “show no sign of significantly altering the likelihood of international warfare”. They cut prediction error by 10.7 percent across 125 disputes and by zero when the observations were 140 years of the system as a whole. A measure of war likelihood based on what each side expects to gain or lose is “consistently significant” for pairs of states already in a dispute. It takes the reduction in prediction error to 32.1 percent. How tightly alliances clustered also mattered statistically in the version that adds the effects of the different factors. They note that “it may be that decision makers have already taken those structural attributes into account” (Bueno de Mesquita and Lalman 1988). On my reading, their measures of how many blocs there are and how tightly allies cluster, built from alliance choices, are also partly strategic choices rather than fixed structure.

My judgment is that both studies estimate strategic interaction without a strategic model. Signorino (1999) shows that two standard methods, logit and probit, can give a misleading account of outcomes that depend on players responding to one another’s choices. They can make the apparent effect of capabilities look statistically strong while misrepresenting how outcomes arose. His analysis leaves open what happens when the same game can sustain more than one outcome or when the game itself differs across systems. Signorino and Tarar (2006) show that a strategic method reverses or reshapes several standard findings in 58 deterrence crises, though not which way a strategic re-estimate of system structure would go. Add three more problems. System structure is itself chosen through alliances and growth. System-level observations are few. And shared norms may matter alongside counts of strength (Schroeder 1992). For superintelligent machines there are no observations at all. So every stability claim here stays strictly conditional.

Part 11. Rival machines protect humans only under specific conditions in the two-machine model

Measures That Depend on Ends recommends many human centers of control and owns the policy measures and their ranking. That recommendation is about human institutions, not about machines. What I add here is a set of conditions under which two rival machines protect humanity in the division model. They are necessary, and with equal war costs also sufficient. Whether similar conditions hold for three or more machines is open.

Assume all-or-nothing seizure, no joint seizure, and no rank prize. Then two rival machines protect a human share beyond what humans could enforce alone only when all three conditions hold together:

  1. Each machine can credibly threaten a general war against the other. Neither is hopeless.
  2. Each machine minds the other’s gains more than humanity’s holdings.
  3. Humanity’s share sits in the window the war costs define. It is large enough to be worth a general war to defend, and small enough not to tempt a general war over the division. For unequal machines, each machine’s best-case condition must hold as well.

Two cautions attach to the third condition. Both machines would like to move humanity’s share to themselves, so the model does not explain how humanity’s share comes to sit inside the window. And guardianship rests on ruling out a joint grab; allowing one would cap safe shares at the seizure cost divided by one minus the rival weight plus twice the human weight, leaving none of the window unless that cap sits above the window’s lower edge, as Part 4 showed. With a rank prize, equal machines also need the prize to be no more than twice the war cost plus twice the tie value for machine peace. Seizure under a rank prize is unsolved, and the prize can both prompt defense outside these conditions and tempt a grab of a small share.

These conditions correspond to four quantities in the model and one assumption about information. They come from the two-machine model and are not a ranking of measures:

  • Keeping every leading system able to check the others corresponds to no machine being hopeless. Because a moderate war cost lets even a 90-to-10 pair meet this condition (with joint seizure ruled out), checking a rival’s grab takes less than strict parity.
  • Raising the cost humans can impose on a seizer is the seizure cost. It stays part of humanity’s weight even when humans cannot win a war. Unlike guardianship, a higher seizure cost raises humanity’s safe share under a single bloc and under mutual deterrence, and never shrinks the safe set between rivals.
  • Keeping humanity’s holdings visible is an assumption of complete information, not a quantity in the model. A defender must see a rival’s grab for its choice to join to be triggered.
  • Favoring kinds of standing that several can share over contests with a single first place corresponds to keeping the rank prize low or raising the tie value toward half of it. This draws on the reading, in Ends, Rank and Conflict, of Larson, Paul, and Wohlforth (2014), who hold that status is “not always zero-sum”.
  • Watching the cost of war between the machines cuts both ways. When war is too cheap relative to the seizure cost, rivalry caps humanity’s safe share below a bloc’s. Raising the war cost lifts the machine-peace ceiling. But it also raises the window’s lower edge and can make a weaker machine hopeless.

Two tensions remain inside the model and cannot be drafted away. First, equal strength is exactly where a prize for strict first place is most dangerous. Second, guardianship needs war between the machines to be affordable enough to threaten, whereas mutual deterrence rules such a war out and ends guardianship. If the threat that guards humanity’s share ever fails and general war follows, humanity risks losing its entire share.

Part 12. What the models leave out, and what would change the answer

Every result here is bounded by what is not modelled, what is not measured, and what is not claimed.

What is not modelled

The basic game has a single round and complete information, with promises kept within the round. It leaves out the dynamic and informational ways bargaining fails, studied in The War Baseline, and it leaves out commitment between machines over time.

With complete information, a credible defense deters a grab without any war. If hidden information or miscalculation ever made guardianship fail and set off the general war, the winner would take humanity’s entire share. That is a tail risk of total loss.

The results say when a peaceful deal exists, and which human shares are safe, up to what ceiling. None of them says which deal inside the safe set is chosen, or how humanity comes to hold a share inside the guardianship window.

In the division game, seizure is all or nothing, and joint seizure and side payments are ruled out. To defend means going to full general war. Cheaper forms of guardianship, such as sanctions, are not modelled.

Several things are left out of the later models. Under mutual deterrence, a patron defending its client by limited war is missing, and so are human casualties from proxy war. For the dominant machine, a rival’s added reason to defend an asset it values is missing, and so is the question of human autonomy in the asset role.

The results on machine peace, guardianship and the deadlock among equals are established only for two machines, and so is the stability of mutual deterrence. The kingmaker-pledge results of Part 6 are likewise established only for two machines. Three or more machines, and many machines facing many human communities, remain open.

What is not measured and not claimed

No quantity in any of these models has been estimated for any real machine system. That includes the rival and human weights, the rank prize and tie value, and the costs of war and seizure. It includes the client value, the cost and destruction of proxy war, and the chances of willingness, rival-building and message delivery. It also includes humans’ resources. A test has been designed, in A Test the Conjecture Could Lose, another paper of mine, but not run.

I do not claim to know which conditions real machines will face. Beyond placing the window of safe shares, its unsafe middle and the bloc comparison relative to Gallop (2016), I make no claim that the formal results are new.

What would change the answer

Seven open questions would shift the conclusions if evidence or fuller models settled them:

  1. Which case real machines are in. The test that would say has been designed but not run.
  2. How decisive war between machines is. If war is highly decisive, a small balancer can tip the outcome when the sides are near equal. In a ratio contest, its swing is limited to its share of strength.
  3. Whether machines can survive each other’s first strike. If redundant copies or distributed weights make general war that ruinous, mutual deterrence replaces guardianship with the client and proxy-war world of Part 7. And if holdings buy no safety against a rival treated as a fixed hazard, a machine with satisfiable wants can accept a split (for a strategic rival, a conjecture).
  4. How strongly captured strength builds on itself on Earth. If captured computing power, energy and code readily turn into more strength on a closed planet, then on my reading the conditions Wohlforth et al. (2007) identify point toward hegemony rather than a lasting balance.
  5. Whether a patron under mutual deterrence would defend a human client by limited war. Credible defense of that kind would loosen the seizure cap that limits patronage.
  6. How human communities and their inboxes behave under pressure. If growing holdings leave rival-building unchanged and reduce neither willingness nor message delivery, the tripwire holds. If the machine can use its growing holdings to make fewer messages get through, that can break the tripwire even when willingness rises.
  7. Shared rules and policy. Over disputes about a policy that cannot be split or settled by dividing resources, Gallop’s (2016) three-player war can reappear even where bargaining over divisible resources would allow peace.

Part 13. What to take away

Protection, exploitation and elimination can all occur in these models, and the number of machines by itself never says which.

Neither a single united bloc nor rivals locked in mutual deterrence fight a general war to guard humanity. When humans have no chance of winning a war against the bloc, their safe share is capped at the seizure cost divided by one plus the bloc’s human weight, up to the whole prize. Under mutual deterrence, without defense by limited war, rivals may court humanity as a client. Patronage then pays at most what humans can defend on their own. The harm of being courted can come through destructive proxy war when limited war is cheap. If a resource race raises the worth of resources, it can also come through dispossession, or, assuming no taking short of it, elimination. A single dominant machine, by the model’s definition, keeps humans only when their value as asset, audience or exhibit meets the gain from eliminating them, less the cost.

In the two-machine model, under all-or-nothing seizure, with no rank prize and no joint grab, rivals keep a share above the bloc’s ceiling safe only under three conditions together. Neither machine is hopeless in a general war. Each minds its rival’s gains more than humanity’s. And the share sits in a window, large enough to be worth defending yet small enough not to tempt war. When war between the machines is cheap relative to the seizure cost, rivalry lowers humanity’s safe ceiling below a bloc’s. Many machines rather than one are neither a guarantee of safety nor a sentence of war. In these models, everything turns on what the machines want, on the cost and technology of conflict between them, and on what humans themselves can defend or withhold.

Where to read more

  • Many Machines, the technical paper this guide retells, with formal definitions, proofs and computed tables in its appendix.
  • Measures That Depend on Ends: the recommendation of many human centers of control, which is a different matter from the rival machines I examine here, and the policy measures and their ranking.
  • The War Baseline: the one-machine, one-humanity bargaining model, its hidden-information and shifting-power failures, and why disputes over policy can still deadlock.
  • Ends, Rank and Conflict: scoring machines by relative shares, the view that concern with standing is to be measured, the computing-power caveat for knowledge-seeking machines, and the point that status is not always zero-sum.
  • Takeoff and Emergence: when follower machines exist and can combine against a leader, and when a leader strikes first.
  • Satiation Is Not Enough: Theorems A and C on when a machine with limited wants can credibly promise to stop, and humanity’s own commitment problem across communities.
  • Changing the Ends: the questioning of humanity as a single player.
  • A Test the Conjecture Could Lose: the designed but unrun test of which case real machines are in.
